title: Reading a Poll Without Being Fooled

steps.body:
"A leads B, 48% to 45%." With a margin of ±3, A's band runs 45–51 and B's runs 42–48. They overlap.

So a truth of 47% for both is perfectly consistent with this poll. The lead is **inside the wobble** — which is what commentators mean, when they are careful, by a statistical tie.

explanationVariants: A's band is 45–51 and B's is 42–48. Any true value in the overlap, such as 47%, fits both — so the poll cannot establish who is ahead.
The 3-point lead is no bigger than the 3-point margin, so it is exactly the size of the noise.

widget.prompt: A: 48%, B: 45%, margin ±3 points. What does the poll support?

options.label: Overlapping bands; no supported leader
options.feedback: Right. A lead no bigger than the margin is a lead the data cannot see.

options.label: Candidate A is the supported leader
options.feedback: That reads the point estimates as if they were exact. Each one is the middle of a band, and the bands overlap heavily.

options.label: Candidate A leads by exactly 3 points
options.feedback: The gap between two wobbling estimates wobbles too — in fact it wobbles MORE than either estimate alone.

options.label: The poll provides no useful information
options.feedback: It is not useless: it rules out a landslide for either side. It simply cannot resolve a 3-point gap at this sample size.

widget.prompt: A leads B, 48% to 45%, with a margin of ±3 points on each. The gap is 3 points and the margin is 3 points — judge what the poll actually supports.

judgeOptions.label: The bands overlap — the poll cannot separate them
judgeOptions.feedback: A runs 45–51 and B runs 42–48. They share 45–48, so a tie, or even B ahead, sits comfortably inside what this poll can see.

judgeOptions.label: A is ahead — the poll shows a real lead
judgeOptions.feedback: That reads the headline number and ignores the band. A 3-point gap with a ±3 margin on each side is exactly the case where the poll cannot tell.

judgeOptions.label: They are exactly tied
judgeOptions.feedback: The poll cannot establish a tie either. It rules out a large lead for either candidate and says nothing more precise than that.

judgeOptions.label: B is ahead
judgeOptions.feedback: B ahead is inside the bands, but so is A ahead. 'Cannot separate' is the honest reading, not a reversal.

widget.successFeedback: The bands overlap, so the poll cannot separate them. A lead smaller than the margin is not a lead — it is a headline.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Compare the bands, not the numbers: A runs 45–51, B runs 42–48, and they share 45–48.

explanationVariants: An honest headline reports the uncertainty rather than hiding it inside a verb like "leads" or "surges".
Movement inside the margin is not movement. Two polls a week apart can differ by several points with nothing having changed.

widget.prompt: Poll 1: A 48%. Poll 2 (a week later): A 50%. Margin ±3 both times. Sort the headlines.

items.label: "A surges 2 points after debate"
items.feedback: A 2-point move sits well inside a ±3 margin. Two polls of the same unchanged electorate routinely differ by this much.

items.label: "A's support is unchanged within the margin of error"
items.feedback: Accurate and dull, which is usually the sign of an honest reading.

items.label: "A now leads with a clear majority"
items.feedback: 50% ± 3 spans 47–53, so it does not establish a majority at all — let alone a clear one.

items.label: "Both polls are consistent with support near 49%"
items.feedback: 49% sits inside both bands, so this is a fair summary of what the two polls jointly allow.

widget.missFeedback: Ask whether the claimed movement is bigger than the margin. If it is not, the movement is noise.
widget.successFeedback: Two of those headlines describe the data; two describe the noise as if it were news.

steps.body:
Three questions to ask any poll, in order:

**Who was asked, and how were they chosen?** (bias — the margin cannot see it)
**How many?** (the margin — how much wobble)
**Is the effect bigger than the margin?** (whether the finding survives its own uncertainty)

Skip the first and the other two are decoration.

explanationVariants: Sampling method comes first, because a broken frame makes every downstream number meaningless — including the margin.
A margin of error computed on a self-selected sample is a precise answer to a question nobody asked.

widget.prompt: Put the three questions in the order that protects you best.

items.label: Is the gap bigger than the margin?

misorderFeedback.feedback: Sample size is the easier question, but it is the second one. A big sample chosen badly is worse than a small sample chosen well.
That checks the arithmetic before checking whether the arithmetic applies. If the sample is biased, comparing the gap with the margin is meaningless.

widget.missFeedback: Bias first (it cannot be fixed later), then sample size, then whether the effect clears the margin.
widget.successFeedback: Method, then size, then significance. Any other order lets a well-computed number smuggle in a broken sample.

hints: The bands are 49–57 and 43–51. Ask which claims survive when the truth could be anywhere inside them.
For "a majority", the question is whether the whole band sits above 50.
explanationVariants: The band for A is 49–57, which dips below 50, so a majority is not established. But A's band (49–57) and B's (43–51) still overlap between 49 and 51, so even the lead is not certain.
A 6-point gap with a 4-point margin on each number is a close call, not a settled one — the two bands share the strip from 49 to 51.

widget.prompt: A: 53%, B: 47%, margin ±4 on each. Which is the most defensible reading?

options.label: A likely lead, no confirmed majority
options.feedback: Right. A's band (49–57) dips under 50, and it still shares ground with B's (43–51). "Probably ahead" is as far as the data reaches.

options.label: A clear majority for candidate A
options.feedback: A's band runs from 49% to 57%, and 49% is not a majority. The point estimate alone cannot establish one.

options.label: A complete statistical tie
options.feedback: That overcorrects. The bands overlap only slightly, so the poll does lean toward A — it just cannot promise it.

options.label: An exact six-point lead for A
options.feedback: The gap between two wobbling numbers wobbles more than either. Quoting it as exact is the mistake this whole lesson is about.

steps.body: Read the band, not the number.
takeaways: A lead smaller than the margin is a lead the poll cannot see — the bands overlap and a tie stays on the table.
The gap between two estimates is noisier than either estimate, so it needs a bigger margin, not the same one.
Ask how people were chosen BEFORE you ask how many — bias cannot be repaired downstream.
steps.teaser: Next: the SHAPE all that wobble builds — the bell curve, its 68-95-99.7 promise, and a ruler called z.

concept.body: Draw both bands before you say anything. If they share any ground, the poll cannot tell you which one is really higher. If they are cleanly apart, it can.

explanationVariants: 55 ± 2 is 53–57 and 46 ± 2 is 44–48. They do not overlap, so the poll does support a real lead.
A 9-point gap with 2-point margins is far bigger than the wobble.

widget.prompt: A: 55% ± 2, B: 46% ± 2. Does the poll support a real lead for A?

options.label: Yes — the bands (53–57 and 44–48) do not overlap.
options.feedback: Right. The gap is much larger than the margin, so it cannot be explained by wobble.

options.label: No — you can never compare two poll numbers.
options.feedback: You can, and here the comparison is clean: the two bands share no ground at all.
